narrative: During the 1940s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture were deeply rooted in tradition and identity. While there is limited documentation available for this specific decade, it is clear that styles such as cornrows, which originated in Africa and continued to be practiced in the diaspora, were an integral part of their cultural heritage. These intricate braids not only protected the hair from damage but also served as a symbol of community and connection to one's roots. Other hairstyles, like Bantu knots, were likely worn by women with kinky hair textures, which were prevalent among people of Sub-Saharan African descent. Although there is no specific mention of these styles in relation to the 1940s, it is probable that they continued to be practiced during this time period. The Jheri curl, a popular hairstyle among Black Americans in the following decades, did not emerge until the 1980s and early 1990s, so its influence on hairstyles during the 1940s would have been negligible. Nonetheless, it is evident that Black and African women's hair culture was rich, vibrant, and deeply connected to their identity and heritage.
